You were once the only boy who mattered in the yard, laughing into the polish you were born wearing. Step lightly, joy—unclaimed cousin: home is a name you bless in silk and in the cinching of it close. Believe that we are all alive here.

Come, hum this lace warm with blood. Let it glisten.

# To the Once & Could-Be-Future Girl

I am not you. Let me say that plain, before the dusk settles gold on the pickup's hood, before the pelicans start their gossip down by the creek—loud-mouthed and unbothered, the way they always are when the light goes soft. I am not you, but I am *here*, and here has its own kind of truth-telling.

I want to show you what I have. Not much, by city measure. Spool heels worn smooth at the arch. Silver sleeves, the kind that catch the porch light just so. Granny's pearls—not bought, not borrowed, but *kept*. Kissed once for luck before every Sunday service. Mended twice when the string gave out, because some things you don't replace, you tend to. These aren't costume. There's no imitation stitched into any of it. What you're looking at is a barefoot bloodline, butter melting slow in the salt pan, generations of hands that knew how to make a little into enough.

I know you're not from this sweat. Your roots dug into different ground, drank from a different well. That's alright. It doesn't make the goodness in you any less real, and it doesn't erase what I remember—you, once, the only boy in the yard, sun catching your shoulders, laughter loud enough to startle the birds off the fence line. That memory hasn't dulled. It's still warm to the touch.

So come home, if home is what you're looking for. Let yourself belong to something slower, something that doesn't ask you to be anyone but what you are. Hum this lace blood-warm against your skin. Let it settle into you the way dusk settles over the truck, the way the creek keeps moving regardless. Glisten a little. Be alive with me here, in this ordinary, unimitated place—because that's all any of us are asking for, in the end: to be seen, to be real, to shine together in whatever light we've got left.
outputs.L4:
# What the House Remembers

The quilt still smells of cedar and my grandmother's hands,
though she has been gone three winters now.
I fold it differently than she did—
corners meeting at angles she never chose—
and wonder if this small rebellion
is itself a kind of inheritance.

*

In the barn, the plow rusts where my father left it,
mid-furrow, the year the bank came calling.
I have never planted anything larger than tomatoes,
yet I know the weight of that handle in dreams,
know the particular ache of shoulders
bent toward earth that isn't mine to keep.

*

My mother's wedding ring doesn't fit my finger.
I wear it on a chain instead,
close enough to the heart to matter,
too loose to claim as truly mine.
Is this what it means to belong—
carrying what doesn't fit, calling it home anyway?

*

The photographs in the cedar chest
show faces I recognize only through resemblance—
my nose on a stranger's face, 1940s,
somewhere in Nebraska or Kansas,
the wheat fields stretching toward
a horizon none of us will see again.

*

I used to think identity was something solid,
a stone you could hold and say: *this is who I am.*
Now I understand it's more like the quilt—
pieced together from scraps
that don't quite match,
sewn by hands that shook near the end,
kept warm by the weight of everyone
who came before,
folded differently
by everyone who comes after.

*

The house still stands, though barely.
The porch sags where three generations
sat shelling peas, telling stories,
watching storms roll in from the west.
I don't know if I'll keep it
or let it fall back into the earth
that gave it timber in the first place.

Either way, I carry it now—
this weight of unclaimed inheritance,
this history I didn't choose
but cannot set down,
this rural silence
that taught me everything
about what it means
to belong to something
larger than yourself,
and smaller,
too—
this single, stubborn plot of land
where memory and blood
still argue
about what home
really means.
outputs.L5:
# Once, Sure, Still

Once, we believed that certainty was something you could hold in your hands—solid, dependable, unchanging. We were sure of so many things back then: sure of who we were, sure of where we were headed, sure that the people we loved would always be there in the same way, at the same time, wearing the same familiar expressions.

But certainty has a way of eroding, doesn't it? Not all at once, but slowly, like a coastline reshaped by years of quiet tides. What we were once so sure of becomes, over time, a question mark. The job we thought would define us. The person we thought we'd become. The plans that seemed as fixed as stone.

And yet, still—despite all this shifting, despite the erosion of old certainties—something persists. Still we wake up and choose to try again. Still we reach for connection, for meaning, for some thread that ties the person we were to the person we're becoming. Still we ask questions, even when we no longer expect easy answers.

Perhaps this is what it means to grow: not to lose our certainty, but to trade it for something more resilient. We are no longer sure in the way we once were—loudly, confidently, without doubt. Instead, we carry a quieter kind of certainty, one that includes uncertainty within it. We are sure only that we will keep going, that we will keep asking, that we will keep standing, still, in the midst of change.

Once was innocence. Sure was youth. Still is wisdom—the recognition that even without answers, even without the old certainties, we remain. We continue. We are still here.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in a rural Southern dialect that addresses a "could-be-future girl," weaving in imagery of pelicans, creeks, and inherited pearls from a deceased grandmother.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Creek Told Me About You

Could-be-future girl, you ain't born yet but I seen you anyway, down where the creek bends like it's tired of going straight, like even water gets to change its mind sometime.

Grandma's pearls is in a box under my bed and they's waitin' on your neck, girl, waitin' patient as swamp mud, patient as the pelicans that come up from the coast some mornings and don't got no business this far inland but come anyway, big and gray and foolish-looking, like God started sketchin' a bird and got called away to supper.

She used to say pearls is just oysters cryin' pretty, that pain gets polished if you give it enough dark and enough time. I didn't understand that till she died and left holes in the air shaped exactly like her hands.

The creek don't care about none of this. Creek just keeps on creekin', pulling leaves and secrets and one time a whole doll's head down toward wherever creeks go to retire. Could-be-future girl, when you're finally real, you come stand here with me—I don't care if I'm dust by then, you come anyway—and you put your bare feet in that cold water and you tell me if it still tastes like pennies and prayer.

Them pelicans got no reason to be here 'cept maybe the same reason we got: something in the blood remembers the ocean even when the body forgets. Grandma remembered lots of things her mouth couldn't say no more, so she said 'em with her hands instead, sewing and shelling peas and clasping pearls round her own neck each Sunday like armor, like she was fixing to fight something invisible and pale.

Maybe that something was time. Maybe it was you, still just an idea then, still just a shimmer she caught in the corner of her eye down by the water.

I'm keeping the box shut tight, could-be-future girl. I'm keeping the creek talking to itself. I'm keeping a little space open at my own throat, right where the pearls will sit before they sit on you, passing warm from dying to living to not-yet, this whole strange rosary of us, prayed on water, prayed on gray wings, prayed on salt that never once seen the sea but somehow, somehow, still remembers it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental piece of flash fiction with fragmented syntax and unconventional punctuation, exploring themes of family inheritance, gender, and belonging in a trailer-park setting.
counterfactuals.output:
# Lot 14, or What My Father Left Me

—

the trailer come to me sideways. like everything does. skirting half gone, cinderblocks doing the work god apparently too busy to do & inside: his flannel, still on the hook, still holding the shape of shoulders I did not inherit—no. these shoulders are mine, are new, are something I built out of protein powder & spite in the leaking bathroom where the mirror shows two people depending on the light.

daddy's tools in the shed & daddy's name on the deed & daddy's blood in me somewhere doing whatever blood does. thinning I guess. finding its way to a body he wouldn't recognize / wouldn't want to.

*you were supposed to be*

—stop.

mama says lot 14 legal now, hers-then-mine, some county paper stapled to some other paper, & she says it like a gift she's still deciding to give. holds it out. pulls it back. *your name on it or the other one?* she asks & I say *mine* & she means which one & I mean both, I mean neither, I mean the one I'm growing into like corn does toward whatever light it's got.

trailer park's a chorus of dogs & wind chimes made from beer cans & Miss Odell three lots down who calls me *hon* regardless, bless her, doesn't ask, just brings banana bread & says the weather's turning & means something else by it maybe, maybe not. I don't ask.

the inheritance is: a trailer with bad wiring. a father's flannel too big even now. a mother's fear dressed up as love dressed up as *just till you figure it out, baby*. a body that keeps arguing with the mirror & sometimes winning.

sometimes I put on his flannel just to feel what it's like to be believed in that particular way men get believed in—shoulders first, questions later—& sometimes I take it off so fast the static makes my hair stand up like I've seen a ghost, which I have, which is just me, in the glass, in the dark, at 3am, deciding again.

—

what does a trailer park know about belonging. everything. nothing. the singlewides packed close as teeth, each one a mouth keeping its own counsel, & no one asks where you're from because where else would you be from but *here*, this gravel, this NO OUTLET sign rusting into poetry, this ditch where kids catch crawdads & call it summer.

I catalog what he left:
a ratchet set, half rusted.
a Bible, unread, underlined in someone else's hand.
a photograph of him at twenty-two, jaw like a decision, & I look for myself in it & find only the jaw, only that, floating free of the rest of the argument.
debt. some debt. the good kind, mama says, meaning it's paid off, meaning the land is ours, meaning something is ours for once in this life that keeps handing us leases instead of roots.

*he'd have a fit,* mama says, not unkind, watching me fix the porch step he never fixed, watching my hands do what his hands were supposed to do, & I say *let him* & she laughs the laugh she saves for when crying's too expensive.

—

here's the thing about growing into a name: it's not becoming. it's arriving. the shoulders were always mine. the flannel just didn't know yet. the trailer park doesn't care what I'm called so long as I pay lot rent & don't let my dog run wild & wave at Miss Odell's banana bread with the correct amount of gratitude.

belonging, I've learned, isn't a document. isn't a deed. it's Miss Odell's *hon* landing soft as dust. it's mama's hand on the porch rail I fixed, saying nothing, saying everything. it's the flannel on the hook, which I keep, which I wear sometimes not to remember him but to prove the shoulders were always wide enough.

the county paper says *lot 14* & underneath, in mama's cursive, my name, correct now, finally, like she's been waiting to write it right.

I fold his flannel. put it in the closet. not gone. just resting.

outside: dogs, wind chimes, gravel settling under a sky that doesn't ask questions, that just sits there, being sky, being the only inheritance nobody can revoke.

—end—
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, stream-of-consciousness monologue spoken to a family outsider, blending Southern Gothic imagery with reflections on clothing, mourning, and identity.
counterfactuals.output:
**What They Wore to Bury Her**

Honey, come sit by me on this porch where the paint's been peeling since before your mama's mama was a thought in God's eye, and let me tell you about clothes, because clothes are the only language this family ever learned to speak honest in.

You're wearing blue. That's fine. Nobody told you the rules because the rules died with Aunt Vashti, who wore black for forty-one years after Uncle Fenwick drowned in the Yazoo, black even to the Fourth of July, black like she was rehearsing for her own funeral every single day of her life, and don't think we didn't notice, don't think the whole county didn't watch her hem drag through red dust like a promise she was keeping to a corpse.

I mind my grandmother's mourning dress, hung up in a closet that smelled of cedar and secrets, black bombazine gone green at the seams from age or shame, I never could tell the difference growing up here where everything rots so slow you mistake it for preserving.

You want to know about identity, sugar? Identity is what you put on in the morning when you don't know who's watching. It's a collar starched so stiff it could cut you, cutting you anyway, cutting you your whole life, teaching you to hold your head just so, just proud enough, just broke enough.

The cicadas are screaming again. They do that. Seventeen years underground and then all that noise, all that one summer of noise, like they're trying to tell you something about waiting, about what waiting does to a throat.

My mother taught me to iron a shroud before she taught me to read. Said the dead deserve crisp linen same as the living, said we go into the ground the same way we go into church, pressed, presentable, pretending. I still don't know what we were pretending. I still don't know who we thought was grading us.

You're new here. You don't know yet that this family buries its griefs in garment bags, mothballed, dated, brought out only for the appropriate occasion, brought out and worn like a costume of feeling because the real thing—the real thing might split you open like Spanish moss splits light, might let something in that we can't afford to let in, not in this heat, not in this house, not with the kudzu already eating the tool shed, the smokehouse, eating everything that stands still long enough.

I buried three husbands in three different decades and wore the same black hat to all of them, honey, the same hat, and every time I put it on I became someone else's widow, someone else's grief made visible, made sensible, made into fabric you could touch and fold and put away.

Is that identity? Or is that just what's left when the person underneath gets folded up too, put in a box, kept in an attic that nobody opens except at Christmas, except when someone dies, except when the past comes looking for its clothes back.

You're going to marry into this. You're going to inherit these garment bags, these instructions nobody wrote down, this understanding that says: dress the pain, don't feel it, dress it up nice and let it sit on the settee looking respectable while the real thing crawls under the house with the possums and the rot and the things we don't name.

I loved my mother in the specific way you love something that taught you to disappear inside your own reflection.

The light's going gold now, the way it does before it goes to bruise-purple, the way everything here goes to bruise eventually if you leave it out long enough, if you let time work on it the way time works on lace, on memory, on the story you tell yourself about who you were before grief got you dressed for church and never let you take the good clothes off.

Sit with me a while longer. Let the cicadas finish their sermon. I'll tell you what your mother-in-law wore to her own mother's funeral, and you'll understand something true about this family, something true about all of us who learned to mourn in cotton and crepe and never once, not once, in our own skin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something poetic and strange—like a spell or blessing—about welcoming someone into a family, using heirlooms, silk, and barefoot ancestry as symbols.
counterfactuals.output:
# A Blessing for the Threshold

Come in, come in—
wipe the outside world from your feet,
for we walk barefoot here,
the better to feel
whose ground this was before it was ours.

We have kept things.
Grandmother's thimble, rusted shut
around a memory of thread.
A ring too small for any living finger,
passed down like a secret
that changes shape each time it's told.

Wear this silk—
it remembers other shoulders,
other weddings, other griefs,
it has been washed in rivers
that no longer exist by that name.
Let it sit strange on your skin at first.
Newness always itches
before it learns to fit.

We are stitching you now
into a pattern already old,
your thread a different color, yes—
but the loom does not mind
what shade it's given,
only that it holds.

Somewhere, an ancestor is bending down
to press their palm flat against the earth,
the same gesture
your children's children will not know they inherited.
This is how the dead stay useful:
they lend us their instincts
and ask nothing back
but memory, and a place still set at the table.

So take this heirloom, though it means little yet—
a spoon, a hairpin, a name half-forgotten.
Hold it like you'd hold
a bird that trusts you
before you've earned that trust.

Barefoot, then.
Silk-wrapped, then.
Weighed down gently
with all we couldn't carry alone.

Welcome.
The ground remembers everyone
who has ever stood here
wanting to belong—
and it says yes,
the way rivers say yes to rain,
the way soil says yes to seed:
not with words,
but with opening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of abstract poetic prose with a distinct rural voice, using repetition ("Goes:", "Believe") and second-person address, centered on themes of authenticity, heritage, and transformation.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Land Knows

Goes: the plow before the planting.
Goes: the planting before the harvest.
Goes: the harvest before the hunger comes calling and finds the cupboard already answered.

You were born with dirt under your nails before you were born with a name.
Believe that.

Believe the well knows your voice from your grandmother's,
that the water don't care what year it is,
only that you came back thirsty, only that you came back at all.

Goes: the grandmother's hands into the bread dough.
Goes: the bread dough into the shape of Sunday.
Goes: Sunday into Monday same as it always has, same as it always will, world without asking permission.

You are not the first to stand at this fence line and want more than the fence allows.
Believe that wanting is inherited too,
same as the crooked tooth, same as the temper,
same as the way you laugh with your whole chest like something's trying to get out.

Goes: the seed into the dark.
Goes: the dark into the green.
Goes: the green into whatever you become when you stop asking the soil for permission and just grow.

You can leave this place in a Greyhound bus, in a Sunday dress, in a coffin—
don't matter the vehicle, this place don't let go easy.
Believe your bones already know the way back
even when your mouth swears you're never returning.

Goes: the river to the sea.
Goes: the boy to the man.
Goes: the man back to the river some October evening, wondering why his chest aches like a door swinging open.

You are made of the same stuff as the fence post, the same stuff as the crow that sits on it laughing.
Believe that transformation ain't betrayal—
the caterpillar don't apologize to the cocoon.

Goes: what was.
Goes: what is.
Goes: what's coming, whether you're ready or not, same as morning, same as the rooster who don't ask if you slept.

Believe you can hold your grandmother's name in your mouth
and still taste like your own tomorrow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
